verdict.rationale: The denial of a stage of cleansing after death for the saved is supported by a convergent lexical pattern. Hebrews 10:14 pairs the perfect indicative (a completed action whose result still stands) 'he has perfected' (tetelEIOken) with 'in perpetuity' (eis to diEnekes), asserting a completed and abiding perfecting of 'the ones being made holy' (tous hagiazomenous). Hebrews 1:3 already names 'having made cleansing of sins' (katharismon tOn hamartiOn poiEsamenos) as a finished act before Christ's session (sitting enthroned) at the right hand. 2 Corinthians 5:8 sets 'to be away from the body' (ekdEmEsai ek tou sOmatos) against 'to be at home with the Lord' (endEmEsai pros ton kyrion) as paired aorist (a completed past action) infinitives with no intermediate stage. Luke 23:43 places 'today' (sEmeron) with 'paradise' (paradeisos) for the dying man. 1 John 1:7 says the blood of Jesus 'cleanses' (katharizei) 'from all sin' (apo pasEs hamartias), scope 'all' (pasEs). Romans 8:1 declares 'no condemnation now' (ouden nyn katakrima) for those in Christ. Philippians 1:23 names 'to depart and be with Christ' (analysai kai syn ChristO einai) as a single state. Luke 16:26 fixes a 'great chasm' (chasma mega) between the two post-death locations. The verdict is medium rather than high because 1 Corinthians 3:13-15 uses 'in fire' (en pyri) of the day of judgment, says 'the wage' (ho misthos) burns and the builder 'will suffer loss' (zEmiOthEsetai), then 'but he himself will be saved, as through fire' (autos de sOthEsetai hOs dia pyros), and Matthew 12:32 names 'it shall not be forgiven... neither in this age nor in the age to come' (ouk aphethEsetai... oute en toutO tO aiOni oute en tO mellonti), a contrast of ages, which a purgatorial (post-death purification) reading has used. The Greek of those texts does not itself require a state of purification for persons, but it also does not foreclose the reading as cleanly as some readers assume.

scripture.force: The verb 'he has perfected' (tetelEIOken) is perfect indicative active (a completed action whose result still stands, expressed as an ongoing simple statement of fact) of 'to perfect' (teleioO), expressing a completed action with abiding result. It governs 'the ones being made holy' (tous hagiazomenous), present passive participle (an ongoing action received by the subject), qualified by the adverbial phrase 'in perpetuity' (eis to diEnekes), for all time. By 'a single offering' (mia prosphora), Christ has perpetually perfected the sanctified. The perfect-tense completeness placed against a perpetual adverb leaves no lexical room for a further after-death completing of the believer's standing before God.

The clause 'having made cleansing of sins' (katharismon tOn hamartiOn poiEsamenos) uses the aorist (a completed past action) middle participle 'having made' (poiEsamenos), treating the cleansing as a completed prior act, and is followed by 'he sat down at the right hand' (ekathisen en dexia), a perfective finite verb of session (the act of taking the enthroned seat). The cleansing precedes the session and is presented as accomplished, not as an open process. The noun 'cleansing' (katharismos) occurs seven times in the canon and here describes Christ's once-for-all priestly act.

The two rare verbs are set in deliberate antithetic (opposing) balance: 'to be away from the body' (ekdEmEsai ek tou sOmatos) and 'to be at home with the Lord' (endEmEsai pros ton kyrion). Both are aorist (completed past action) active infinitives expressing a single transition. The clause names no intervening third location or process between departure from the body and being at home with the Lord, so the lexical structure treats the move as immediate.

Paul's phrase 'having the desire to depart and to be with Christ' (tEn epithymian echOn eis to analysai kai syn ChristO einai) joins two articular (with the article 'the') infinitives with a single 'and' (kai). The aorist (completed past action) 'to depart' (analysai), and the present (ongoing simple action) 'to be' (einai), name departure and being-with-Christ as immediately conjoined, with no third stage between them. The preposition 'with' (syn) marks personal presence rather than a staged approach.

The temporal adverb 'today' (sEmeron) is joined to the future 'you will be' (esE), with 'with me' (met emou), 'in paradise' (en tO paradeisO). The dying man, with no remaining opportunity for works or purgation (purification), is promised same-day presence with Christ in 'paradise' (paradeisos). The lexical force locates the destination at the day of death, not after a process. The classical punctuation question, whether 'today' (sEmeron) attaches to 'I say' (legO) or to 'you will be' (esE), is not a manuscript variant.

The verb 'cleanses' (katharizei) is present indicative active (an ongoing, simple statement of fact), and its object phrase is 'from all sin' (apo pasEs hamartias), governed by the blood of Jesus, 'the blood of Jesus' (to haima IEsou). The cleansing agent is the blood of Christ and its scope is 'all' (pasEs) sin. The lexical sweep, all sin, locates the cleansing in Christ's finished provision applied now to the one walking in the light, not in a later after-death purging.

The clause 'therefore now no condemnation' (ouden ara nyn katakrima) fronts the negation 'nothing' (ouden) with the temporal 'now' (nyn) applied to those 'in Christ Jesus' (en ChristO IEsou). The noun 'penal sentence' (katakrima) occurs only three times in the canon, all in Romans. The present, now, abolition of any penal sentence for those in Christ removes the lexical premise for an after-death penal satisfaction by the believer.

The noun 'chasm' (chasma) is a hapax (a word that occurs only once in the entire Bible) in the canon, occurring only here. It is qualified by 'a great one has been fixed' (mega estEriktai), with the perfect passive (a completed action whose result still stands, in passive voice) 'has been fixed' (estEriktai) of 'to fix' (stErizO), treating the gulf as permanently established between the two after-death locations. The lexical force is of a fixed and impassable divide between the after-death states, with no third middle ground named.

Hebrews 9:27 sets 'to die' (apothanein), an aorist (completed past action) infinitive, against 'and after this judgment' (meta de touto krisis). The sequence is death then judgment, with no purgative (purifying) middle term named in the clause. The absence of a lexical stage between dying and 'judgment' (krisis) reinforces an immediate transition rather than a graduated after-death purification.

complicating_texts.resolution: This is the strongest in-canon text used to ground a purgatorial (after-death purification) reading. The Greek says 'the fire itself will test what sort each one's work is' (hekastou to ergon hO opoion estin to pyr autO dokimasei). The agents and patients are explicit: 'fire' (pyr) tests 'work' (ergon), and the result for the builder is 'the wage' (ho misthos) that 'remains' (menei), or 'will be burned up' (katakaEsetai). Then 'if anyone's work is burned up he will suffer loss, but he himself will be saved, as through fire' (ei tinos to ergon katakaEsetai, zEmiOthEsetai, autos de sOthEsetai, hOs dia pyros). Lexically the burned object is 'work' (ergon) and the saved object is 'he himself' (autos), the person, with a clear noun shift between them. The verb 'will suffer loss' (zEmiOthEsetai) is the same lemma (dictionary form) Paul uses in Philippians 3:8 for losing things, not for being purged. The phrase 'through fire' (dia pyros) is escape idiom for narrow rescue from danger, parallel to Amos 4:11, Zechariah 3:2, Jude 1:23. A purgatorial reading is possible if one treats 'fire' (pyr) as a stage the person passes through, but the noun shift from 'work' (ergon) to 'he himself' (autos), the person, in the saved-clause is the lexical hinge, and the passage is set 'on the Day' (en tE hEmera), the end-time day of judgment, not an after-death interval before it.

Jesus says 'it shall not be forgiven him either in this age or in the age to come' (ouk aphethEsetai autO oute en toutO tO aiOni oute en tO mellonti). A purgatorial reading argues that the 'in the coming age' (en tO mellonti aiOni) clause implies some sins ARE forgiven in the age to come, which only makes sense if there is an after-death state where forgiveness is still in view. Lexically the construction is an emphatic universal negation, 'neither... nor' (oute... oute), a Greek idiom for total exclusion in any frame whatever, comparable to John 14:17 'neither sees nor knows' (ouk theOrei auto oude ginOskei). It need not assert that some sins ARE forgiven in the coming age; it can simply close every conceivable temporal scope. The verse does not name an intermediate purgative state. It is consistent with, but does not require, the inference.

Second Maccabees 12, in which Judas Maccabeus arranges sacrifice 'for the dead' (peri tOn tethnEkotOn), that they might be loosed from sin, is historically the principal explicit prooftext for after-death purgation. It lies outside the sixty-six-book canon this engine treats as Scripture, so it is excluded on canon-scope grounds and not on reinterpretation grounds. Its absence from the lexical corpus is itself the reason no purgatorial vocabulary is preserved in the in-canon Greek.

variants.note: The input bundle reports not_in_ecm_scope true and supplies an empty variant_units list. The cited verses lie outside the published CBGM (the Coherence-Based Genealogical Method, the technique used to construct the critical edition of the New Testament text) scope. The well-known Luke 23:43 punctuation question, whether 'today' (sEmeron) attaches to 'I say' (legO) or to 'you will be' (esE), is a punctuation and accentuation issue, not a manuscript text variant. No examined variant unit materially affects the death-then-rest pattern.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Hebrews 10:14 perfect (completed action whose result still stands) 'he has perfected' (tetelEIOken) with 'in perpetuity' (eis to diEnekes), Hebrews 1:3 finished 'cleansing' (katharismon) prior to session (the act of taking the enthroned seat), 2 Corinthians 5:8 paired 'to be away from' (ekdEmeO) and 'to be at home with' (endEmeO) without middle term, Philippians 1:23 'to depart and be with Christ' (analysai kai syn ChristO einai) as one transition, Luke 23:43 'today in paradise' (sEmeron en paradeisO), 1 John 1:7 'cleanses from all sin' (katharizei apo pasEs hamartias), Romans 8:1 'no condemnation now' (ouden nyn katakrima), and Luke 16:26 'a great chasm has been fixed' (chasma mega estEriktai) together yield a spread-across-the-whole-Bible pattern of completed cleansing now and immediate presence with Christ at death, with no in-canon Greek term for a purgative (purifying) intermediate state for the saved.

1 Corinthians 3:13-15 sets 'work' (ergon) and 'he himself' (autos) in the same end-time scene with 'to be saved as through fire' (sOzesthai hOs dia pyros), and the participant most naturally has the fire as something the person passes through, even if the burning object is 'work' (ergon). Matthew 12:32 names 'in this age' (en toutO tO aiOni) and 'in the coming age' (en tO mellonti aiOni) in a forgiveness frame that some readers take to imply continuing forgiveness in the next age, which would require a state in which forgiveness still applies. Read together with the deuterocanonical (books from the Greek Old Testament that the engine excludes from the sixty-six-book canon) 2 Maccabees 12:43-45, these have grounded a long reading of an after-death purgative stage for the saved. The lexical objection is that the Greek of 1 Corinthians 3 shifts noun between burned object ('work', ergon) and saved object ('he himself', autos), and Matthew 12:32 is an emphatic universal negation rather than a positive claim about the coming age, so the Greek does not require the purgatorial reading but it does not foreclose it as sharply as some readers claim.

A minority reading takes 2 Corinthians 5:8 'to be at home with the Lord' (endEmEsai pros ton kyrion) and Philippians 1:23 'to be with Christ' (syn ChristO einai) as deferred to the resurrection, with the body of texts using 'to sleep' (koimaO) of the dead, as in 1 Thessalonians 4:13-15 and John 11:11, taken to imply an unconscious interim. Lexically the verbs 'to be away from' (ekdEmeO) and 'to be at home with' (endEmeO) in 2 Corinthians 5 are paired with no third state, which weighs against the soul-sleep reading rather than for purgation; included here only to acknowledge it as a separate competing lens that this verdict also denies.

hermeneutics.notes: The verdict turns on grammatical tense, the perfect (completed action whose result still stands) 'he has perfected' (tetelEIOken), the present (ongoing simple action) 'cleanses' (katharizei), the 'now' of Romans 8:1, the antithetic (opposing) pairing of 'to be away from' (ekdEmeO) and 'to be at home with' (endEmeO), and the noun-shift between 'work' (ergon) and 'he himself' (autos) in 1 Corinthians 3:13-15. Analogia scripturae (interpreting Scripture by Scripture) harmonizes the in-canon witnesses, which do not name a purgative (purifying) middle state in any positive lexical construction, though 1 Corinthians 3:15 'through fire' (dia pyros) is read in opposite ways.

stem_audit.neutralized_form: Whether believers who die in Christ pass immediately to glory, or undergo an after-death process of purgation (purification) before glory, is the question; the original stem's phrases immediately and finally purified in His finished work, and not progressively purified in an after-death state of purgation, load the denial of purgatory into the stem.
stem_audit.notes: The stem encodes the conclusion by contrasting immediate-and-final purification against after-death progressive purgation (purification). The verdict above is derived on the original stem from the lexical data, but the neutralized form states the underlying either-or so the grammar, not the framing, carries the weight. Confidence is medium rather than high because 1 Corinthians 3:13-15 and Matthew 12:32 supply genuine lexical hooks for the purgatorial reading even if the Greek does not require it. No web fallback was used.

lay_summary: This question asks whether a believer who dies is fully cleansed at once through Christ's finished work, or must pass through a later process of purification before reaching glory. Several lines of Greek vocabulary lean toward immediate cleansing. Hebrews 10:14 uses a perfect-tense verb (a completed action whose result still stands) meaning 'he has perfected' (tetelEIOken), joined to a phrase meaning 'in perpetuity' (eis to diEnekes), said of 'the ones being made holy' (tous hagiazomenous). Hebrews 1:3 describes Christ as having made 'cleansing of sins' (katharismon) before sitting at the right hand, treating the cleansing as already accomplished. Second Corinthians 5:8 pairs two rare verbs, 'to be away from the body' (ekdEmEsai) and 'to be at home with the Lord' (endEmEsai), with nothing named between them. Philippians 1:23 says Paul desires 'to depart and to be with Christ' (analysai kai syn ChristO einai) in a single phrase. Luke 23:43 promises the dying man same-day presence with Christ in 'paradise' (paradeisos). First John 1:7 says the blood of Jesus 'cleanses from all sin' (katharizei apo pasEs hamartias), using a wide word for 'all' (pasEs). Romans 8:1 says there is now 'no condemnation' (ouden katakrima) for those in Christ. Luke 16:26 names a great fixed 'chasm' (chasma) between the two after-death states. The picture leaves no in-canon term for a stage of purgative (purifying) cleansing between death and glory. Two complicating texts qualify the verdict. First Corinthians 3:13 to 15 says 'fire' (pyr) will test each builder's 'work' (ergon) on the day of judgment, the work may be burned up, and the builder himself will be 'saved as through fire' (sOthEsetai hOs dia pyros). The Greek shifts nouns between the burned object, the work, and the saved object, the person ('he himself', autos), but the picture of a person passing through fire is real and has been read as purgative. Matthew 12:32 says a sin 'will not be forgiven' (ouk aphethEsetai) 'in this age or in the age to come' (en toutO tO aiOni oute en tO mellonti), which has been read to imply some sins are forgiven in the next age, requiring a state where that forgiveness applies. The Greek of these texts allows but does not require a purgative reading, since the noun shift in First Corinthians 3 separates the burned work from the saved person, and Matthew 12:32 is an emphatic total exclusion rather than a positive claim about the coming age. So the lexical pattern supports the denial of after-death purgation, but the room left by these two texts is the honest reason readers diverge.
